input.query: Do the authors offer a hypothesis for why Twitter data makes better predictions about the inventory of languages used in each country?

output.reason: The evidence provides a hypothesis: the Discussion attributes differences in population representation to Twitter representing more wealthy populations (matching better with GDP-weighted populations and worse with internet-usage-weighted populations), with the alternate interpretation that the Twitter collection is based on urban areas with wealthier populations. The Population Demographics section also notes that English and Spanish are very common on Twitter, so countries predominantly using these languages are well represented by default, and that Twitter shows more false positives (over-predicted languages) in several countries, indicating more diverse apparent language populations.

claims.text: The abstract states that Twitter data makes better predictions about the inventory of languages used in each country.
The discussion reports that not all languages from censuses are found in digital texts, and in this case Twitter has fewer missing languages.

The paper notes that Twitter provides a better representation of North America and Oceania, while the two corpora agree in many cases for Europe, parts of Africa with ground-truth data, and South America.

The authors note that many countries have only a few languages, so a high true positive rate could reflect only one or two languages; for example, English and Spanish are very common on Twitter, so countries predominantly using these languages will have good representation by default.

For false positives, the authors state that more research is needed to distinguish between immigration, tourism, and business as alternate sources of false positive languages appearing in digital data sets.

Regarding differences between Twitter and web-crawled data, the authors hypothesize that Twitter as a platform represents more wealthy populations than general web-crawled data, and offer an alternate interpretation that the Twitter collection is based on urban areas, which tend to have more wealthy populations.

The supplied evidence does not include a hypothesis specifically explaining why Twitter data makes better predictions about the inventory of languages in each country; the paper reports this as a finding and offers hypotheses about representativeness of populations more generally.
